output.headline: Noah Woods’s family remember ‘the happy little boy that he was’
output.bodyHtml:
About 1,300 members of the public joined the search for Noah Woods, a three-year-old boy who was found dead in a pond after going missing from a playground. He had left the play area ‘through a gap in the fence’, an inquest heard.

Suffolk police said Noah became separated from a relative after visiting the playground in Merriam Close, Brantham, on the afternoon of 15 September.

Police said Noah, who had been undergoing an assessment for autism, was non-verbal and partially deaf.

Met police divers recovered his body from what is known locally as Decoy Pond on the afternoon of 16 September. Suffolk police said his death was not being treated as suspicious.

Noah’s family said they would like him to be remembered as ‘the happy little boy that he was’, after the inquest into his death was opened and adjourned in Ipswich on Friday.

In a statement, they said: ‘Noah was a happy, cheeky, playful three-year-old boy who loved to laugh, loved to giggle and who brought joy wherever he went. He was part of a loving and caring family, living with his mummy, daddy and his little baby brother. He was at the centre of our world.

‘Noah was being assessed for autism, although he had not received a diagnosis. He also had mild hearing loss and was speech delayed.

‘Despite the challenges he faced, he was learning every day. He was saying new words all the time and had only just started finding and using his little voice. One of the things we miss most is the special sound of his voice. It was unique, wonderful, and something we will carry with us forever.’

The statement said Noah was ‘the most affectionate’ boy who had an ‘incredibly special’ bond with his brother.

DCI Matthew Connick told the inquest that on 15 September Noah, of East Bergholt, Suffolk, was being ‘looked after by relatives and this was part of a normal routine for Noah’.

He said they walked to an under-fives play area, where CCTV footage in the park ‘showed Noah playing with his relative’. The first piece of footage was timed at 2.13pm and he was last seen playing at 2.37pm, said Connick, who added that the CCTV was motion-activated so did not provide continuous footage.

He said the relative, who was not named at the hearing, had provided a statement to police. The officer said Noah ‘left through a gap in the fence leading to the memorial garden where he left through an open gate’. He said Noah went in the direction of Decoy Pond and was ‘being closely followed by his relative who was trying to keep up with him’.

He said the relative ‘shouted after him’ but after 200 metres Noah could not be seen. ‘Police were called and a large-scale search operation began,’ Connick said.

A Met police diver found Noah ‘approximately 5 metres from the bank and within submerged tree roots’. The depth was estimated at 1.8 metres at that point, he added.

Paramedics confirmed Noah’s death at 4.31pm and his mother, Charlie Peck, formally confirmed his identity at Ipswich hospital that evening. A postmortem examination at Addenbrooke’s hospital mortuary in Cambridge recorded his medical cause of death as pending further investigation, Connick said.

The Suffolk assistant coroner Jyoti Gill said at the outset of the hearing, which was not attended by the boy’s family: ‘I would like to express my deepest condolences to Noah’s family and friends and all those affected by Noah’s death.’

She said at the end of the six-minute hearing: ‘The inquest is adjourned to a date to be fixed in due course.’

Noah’s father, Rhys Woods, had paid tribute to his son in a message shared on a community Facebook group last week, describing Noah as the ‘sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give’. He added: ‘We are going to miss him so very much.’

Football players paid tribute to Noah by wearing black armbands during Everton’s home match against Ipswich Town on Saturday.
output.standfirst: About 1,300 people joined the search for the ‘happy, cheeky, playful’ three-year-old, who was found dead in a pond after leaving a Suffolk playground through a gap in the fence, an inquest heard
output.progress: About 1,300 members of the public joined the search for Noah, and the assistant coroner Jyoti Gill opened an inquest in Ipswich on Friday.

output.headline: Court refuses bail to far-right activist Daniel Thomas over Channel dinghy
output.bodyHtml:
Magistrates have refused bail to the far-right agitator Daniel Thomas, who was filmed apparently slashing a boat in the Channel with a blade while an emergency responder was onboard and has pleaded not guilty to causing criminal damage.

Thomas, 37, appeared at Basingstoke magistrates court on Friday morning, where he also pleaded not guilty to failing to disclose to police the pin number of his phone, under section 53 of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000.

The prosecutor Kevin Lucie said Thomas was arrested at a BP service station and taken into custody, where police seized his mobile phone but he allegedly refused to provide the pin code.

Outlining the basis of the criminal damage charge, Lucie alleged Thomas slashed an adrift boat with a knife.

He told the court: ‘On 22 September, around 4.30pm, the defendant on his social platform livestreamed himself from a boat on the English Channel. He broadcast to a significant number of people a boat of migrants being supported by the RNLI in the English Channel. It was a single Rib [rigid inflatable boat] which was adrift.

‘He armed himself with a knife. He slashed the boat.’

Asked about the boat, Lucie confirmed he was unsure if the damage was worth more or less than £5,000, and said: ‘Unfortunately, it is the case that it did go back to France. We have asked for the cost of the damage.’

Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, is a father of four described as a professional roofer. He was seen dabbing his eyes with a tissue at one point during the hearing.

He appeared for the hearing via video link, wearing a black top and grey coat, and spoke only to confirm his name and date of birth. His teenage son and fellow far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known as Tommy Robinson, supported him in court. Other supporters were placed in a separate room to watch a live stream from the court, a routine measure when interest in a case outstrips the space available in a courtroom.

Police kept a visible presence, with an officer in the public gallery of the courtroom, another at the courtroom door and a third in the seated waiting area outside the courtroom.

Dozens of police officers could be seen on Thursday evening monitoring several hundred people, many wearing black, who gathered outside a police investigation centre in Basingstoke, apparently in the belief Thomas was inside. The protest continued for several hours.

A hearing will take place in Portsmouth crown court on Tuesday 29 September, after Thomas said he would like a crown court trial. His lawyer, Simon Pentol KC, said: ‘This defendant is not charged with an offence of political activism, whether you agree with it or not, that is not the issue. He has elected crown court trial over criminal damage simplicita and nothing more, and for not acquiescing to a notice requiring him to provide a pin number.’

He added: ‘I invite this court to bear in mind it’s dealing with a 37-year-old man who lives with his long-standing partner and their four children, all aged between 18 and three, his partner is pregnant once again, four months. She is a full-time mother, he is the full-time provider, or breadwinner, as they used to say.

‘He is a professional roofer by trade. He is, therefore, having to look after his family who, through his political activism, have been under huge threat and due to publication of his mother’s home address, she has had to move home.’
output.standfirst: Thomas, 37, faces a Portsmouth crown court hearing on 29 September after pleading not guilty to criminal damage; he was filmed apparently slashing a boat in the Channel while an emergency responder was onboard
output.progress: The prosecutor Kevin Lucie set out the criminal damage case in court, and a hearing will take place at Portsmouth crown court on 29 September.

context.text: The Crown Prosecution Service decided to prosecute Daniel Thomas following an investigation by Hampshire constabulary into an incident on Tuesday 22 September.

output.headline: Labour’s manifesto author Ravinder Athwal brought in to strengthen Healey’s budget team
output.bodyHtml:
Ravinder Athwal, the economist who wrote Labour’s 2024 manifesto, is taking on a senior role as an adviser to John Healey, bringing Treasury and Downing Street experience to the chancellor’s team in a move likely to fuel speculation about an early general election.

The chancellor is keen to strengthen his team before the critical budget on 28 October, as the economy is buffeted by high oil prices and rising government borrowing costs.

Healey has recruited Athwal as his senior special adviser from the business advisory group Flint Global, previously run by Andy Burnham’s chief of staff, the former Blair-era cabinet minister James Purnell.

Athwal, a Cambridge economics graduate, was closely associated with drawing up Labour’s manifesto and devising Keir Starmer’s five “missions”, which were meant to shape Labour’s approach to government. He worked as a senior economic adviser in Starmer’s Downing Street team but left after a year to join Flint Global.

Related: The man behind the manifesto: Labour’s quiet policy chief

A source close to Healey said: “Having Rav join John’s team as an experienced heavyweight economist at the Treasury ahead of this budget will be invaluable. His political nous will add to the special adviser team, providing John with guidance and counsel to the chancellor.”

Athwal’s presence on Healey’s team could be seen as a strength if the prime minister decides to draw up a fresh manifesto. Suggestions inside Westminster have been growing that Burnham is considering a snap general election after a recent bounce in the polls.

As well as strengthening the snap election rumours, Athwal’s arrival is likely to increase concerns among some in Labour that the Treasury’s instinctive caution is fuelling a “continuity Starmer” approach to economics.

Starmer’s team saw the pledge at the heart of the manifesto, not to increase income tax, national insurance or VAT, as key to Labour’s landslide victory two years ago. But it is widely agreed that it has restricted the party’s room for manoeuvre once in power.

People with knowledge of Athwal’s thinking suggest he has learned from the travails of Labour’s early months in office, however. One left-of-centre economist said: “I’d say he was at the more interesting and curious end of the Starmerite project.”

Before joining Labour, Athwal was a Treasury civil servant, rising to be head of growth strategy. One former colleague described him as “nice and clever – a good combination”.

After taking over at the Treasury in July, Healey hired Will Straw, who played a leading role in the remain campaign during the Brexit referendum, as his chief of staff; some of Rachel Reeves’s economic advisers, including Spencer Thompson, stayed on.

Reeves’s chief economic adviser, the former Clean Bandit violinist Neil Amin-Smith, who was closely involved in her plans to devolve more tax revenue to local leaders, has moved across to Burnham’s No 10.

Athwal is expected to arrive in post next week, a month before Healey’s first budget.

Healey faces a series of tough decisions, with inflation and borrowing costs expected to have wiped out at least half of the headroom Reeves had built up against Labour’s fiscal rules.

He has promised to maintain a “buffer against uncertainty”, though this is widely expected to be significantly smaller than the £24bn in the spring forecast.

Government sources say Healey wants this to be a “focused” budget, after Reeves used her two budgets as chancellor to increase taxes by £70bn a year. Depending on the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts, restoring the cushion in full would be likely to require large tax rises or spending cuts.

Key decisions about future tax and spending appear likely to be held over until a Treasury spending review next year, which will come after Burnham has set out his long-term priorities in a 10-year plan, expected after the budget.

Healey has made clear he does not intend to set a timetable at the budget for when the UK will spend 3% of gross domestic product on defence, for example – a target he insisted, when he resigned from Starmer’s government in June, must be met by 2030.

Treasury sources have said officials are working “at pace” on options for consumer support, as persistently high global oil and gas prices put hopes of a low-key budget under pressure and make it likely that the energy price cap, which determines UK consumer bills, will rise sharply in January.

That help is expected to fall far short of the costly universal approach taken by Liz Truss in 2022.

Flint Global was approached for comment.
output.standfirst: Athwal is expected to arrive next week, a month before a critical budget, with the economy buffeted by high oil prices and rising borrowing costs; the move is likely to fuel early election speculation
output.progress: Treasury sources have said officials are working ‘at pace’ on options for consumer support, with the energy price cap likely to rise sharply in January.

output.headline: Court hears victims’ accounts at pre-sentencing hearing for ex-DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson
output.bodyHtml:
A court heard on Friday how two women sexually assaulted by Jeffrey Donaldson when they were children have been affected by the abuse, and that the former leader of the Democratic Unionist party in Northern Ireland should be sent to prison for more than 10 years.

The disgraced politician, who headed the DUP between 2021 and 2024, was found guilty in June of 18 counts of sexual abuse against the women, including one count of rape.

Donaldson is expected to be sentenced next month.

Recounting the case, Rosemary Walsh KC reminded Judge Paul Ramsey how the distress felt by Complainant B while giving evidence was “palpable” in the court room.

Referring to a victim statement already with the judge, she told how Complainant B had described the trial as “a terrible experience” and how the abuse she suffered as a child “affected her every day” of her life.

Sometimes she struggled so much she “wishes she could die”, Walsh said, adding that as a result of the abuse she “does not know what love and trust really is”.

The other victim, Complainant A, wrote in her victim impact statement that she felt her childhood had been “stolen from her” and this had led to feelings of shame and anger.

Her sleep and sense of wellbeing were affected to this day and sometimes she felt burnt out from the emotional stress.

Walsh set out the various tariffs for the offences, several of which carried a maximum sentence of two years, but others which carried a maximum sentence of between 10 and 14 years under historic tariffs for crimes, she told the court.

She said historic legislation did not differentiate between a child and an adult victim in all the counts, so the disparity in age between Donaldson and his victims should be considered an “aggravating” factor in sentencing.

She pointed out that Complainant B was “nine or 10” during some of the offending by Donaldson when he was 25 or 26 years old. She had described how she felt “sick” when he abused her and “wanted to scream out” but thought it was her fault.

Complainant B suffered other types of sexual assault by Donaldson when she was as young as “seven or eight”.

Donaldson, 63, who is planning to appeal, sat stony-faced throughout the 70-minute pre-sentencing hearing in Newry courthouse.

Kieran Vaughan KC urged the judge to take into account several “mitigating” factors including Donaldson’s current age and that he was a man of “previous good character”.

He also told the court “there was no offending of this type” in the past 18 years and during this time Donaldson had significant achievements which were “obliterated” by the conviction.

Donaldson’s wife, Eleanor, has already lodged an appeal against the court’s finding that she had committed acts alleged in relation to five of the charges he had faced.

She was found unfit to stand trial on mental health grounds, meaning the jury was asked to find out if she did or did not commit the acts of which she was accused.

She cannot be sent to jail but is appealing to have the court conclusions overturned.
output.standfirst: The women’s statements set out how childhood abuse by Donaldson, 63, found guilty of 18 counts including rape, affected their lives; he should be jailed for more than 10 years, the court heard
output.progress: Rosemary Walsh KC told Judge Paul Ramsey the age gap should be considered an aggravating factor; Donaldson is expected to be sentenced next month.

context.text: The DUP joined other parties in welcoming the verdict against Donaldson and stressed that it had suspended him when he was first charged in 2024.

output.headline: Home Office steps up protection for mosques with record security funding
output.bodyHtml:
The Home Office issued a record £66m of emergency security funding for mosques and related community sites in the UK when violent disorder spread in the aftermath of the Southport attacks in 2024.

Exclusive figures obtained by the Guardian also reveal that a record of about £41m of security funding was issued for mosques and related community sites for the year from April 2025-26 as part of the protective security scheme.

The Home Office said it was working to process all applications for security funding as soon as possible. “To help protect Muslim communities from the appalling levels of hate crime they face, the government has made £40m available through protective security schemes. This is part of a record £77.4m investment in security funding for faith communities in 2026-27,” a spokesperson said.

The government launched a security scheme for places of worship in 2016 for England and Wales, and later created a dedicated scheme worth £29.4m for mosques and faith schools in the UK in 2023 to provide security to ensure the safety of Muslim communities.

Security funding issued for mosques, Islamic faith schools and associated sites rose from £73,147 in 2016-17 to about £3m in 2022-23, £29m in 2024-25 and a record of about £41m in 2025-26, according to figures obtained via a freedom of information request.

The Home Office introduced a separate emergency security scheme as a temporary measure for places of worship when violent disorder spread across cities after a knife attack in Southport in 2024 in which three girls at a dance class were murdered.

About £66m of the almost £69m granted to places of worship in the UK as part of this scheme was issued to mosques and associated sites, the data revealed. At the time, mosques and hotels housing asylum seekers were targeted after false news had spread online claiming that the perpetrator of the attack was a Muslim asylum seeker.

Akeela Ahmed, the chief executive of the British Muslim Trust, the government’s partner for monitoring anti-Muslim hatred, said the figures “tell an incredibly sombre story about the rise in anti-Muslim hostility that British Muslims are living with”.

“Security needs are increasing as a direct response to the increase in attacks that mosques are under,” Ahmed said. “If we want to bring down the costs for protecting British Muslims in the UK then we need to reduce the need for protection and address the root causes of hate against Muslim communities.”

In July the trust published data showing that across Britain one mosque was attacked every five days in the past year.

Shaista Gohir, the chief executive of Muslim Women’s Network UK, said the figures created “the impression that substantial action is being taken to tackle anti-Muslim hostility” but the government’s response remained “limited compared with the scale of the problem”.

“There is little visible action to address the safety of Muslim women and most of the funding doesn’t even appear to reach mosques or other community sites. One mosque leader I spoke to recently had to apply several times and still only received funding for some requested measures. Many others are still waiting for decisions,” Gohir said.

The Jami community centre in Birmingham has introduced its own security measures, including gates and blackout boards, while it completes its application for security funding. The centre has reported at least five incidents relating to hate crime and racially aggravated criminal damage between March and July this year, according to West Midlands police.

Worshippers told the Guardian about the incidents – some of which had not been reported to police – including smashed windows and Islamophobic graffiti.

Khalid, a volunteer at the centre, organised an emergency meeting with MPs, councillors and police. He criticised the lack of response from West Midlands police to the several incidents that have occurred.

“We’ve had the Prevent team from the council coming here. We’ve had the imam being verbally abused. There’s people being verbally abused … What are we waiting for? Like a disaster to happen?,” he said.

He added: “The centre feels that they’re not being supported enough. More needs to be done. No one should ever feel unsafe coming to pray. It’s not safe. They feel insecure in their own home and in their own place of worship.”

Islam, a 41-year-old private hire driver who attends the centre, reported one incident to the police earlier this year, when an individual shouted abuse at worshippers.

He said the attacks had forced many female worshippers and children to attend another mosque nearby due to fears for their safety. “I don’t think any Muslim hijabi lady would walk to this centre on their own,” Islam said.

Paulette Hamilton, the MP for Birmingham Erdington, said she was “deeply concerned” by the attacks on the centre. “It’s absolutely hateful. I think the people who are doing it are cowardly and there is no place for that sort of thing in the constituency,” she said.

West Midlands police said they remained in “close contact with leaders and worshippers” at the Jami community centre. “We take all forms of hate crime seriously, and every report of it made to us is investigated as we work to bring offenders to justice,” a spokesperson said.
output.standfirst: A record £66m was issued for mosques after the Southport disorder, but the government’s anti-Islamophobia partner says rising security sums reflect growing hostility, with one mosque attacked every five days
output.progress: The Home Office has made £40m available to protect Muslim communities, part of a record £77.4m faith security investment for 2026-27.

output.headline: Jay-Z’s denial backed by woman who now says she never met him
output.bodyHtml:
A woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her when she was 13 years old has said that she has never met the rap superstar, and has formally withdrawn her allegation.

The unnamed woman had originally made the allegation in a lawsuit filed in 2024, claiming that Jay-Z, real name Shawn Carter, had drugged and raped her with Sean Combs, known as P Diddy. The incident was alleged to have happened at a party after an MTV awards ceremony in 2000.

Jay-Z denied the allegations, describing them as a blackmail attempt, and Combs also denied them. Jay-Z’s lawyer maintained the events relied on an “impossible timeline”. The woman dropped the lawsuit in 2025, and Jay-Z filed a counter suit.

As that lawsuit progresses, the woman has now said her claims were false. “Shawn ‘Jay-Z’ Carter never raped me. I have never met or spoken to Mr Carter. Mr Carter never engaged in any inappropriate conduct toward me whatsoever,” she said in a declaration obtained by Rolling Stone.

She added that there was “no truth to any of my claims against Mr Carter. I understand my false accusations have caused Mr Carter immense pain, suffering, and damage that can never be fully undone.”

The woman’s current lawyer, James Blair Newman Jr, said: “Our client maintains that she was a victim of sexual assault, but she was entirely mistaken in her allegations identifying Mr Carter.”

The woman has now been dropped from Jay-Z’s lawsuit, though the rapper is still pursuing her former lawyers, claiming they should have known the allegations were “contradicted by publicly available information, internally inconsistent, and unsupported by any credible story or investigation”. Earlier this month, as they made a motion to have the lawsuit dismissed, lawyer Tony Buzbee and his co-counsel described it as “a malicious prosecution”.

Regarding the woman’s new statement, Buzbee told Rolling Stone: “If for some reason now she is claiming she lied to us and the court, that’s new information.”

Continuing her statement, the woman said memories of sexual assault were triggered by seeing an advertisement calling for victims of Combs to come forward. Combs was being investigated for a number of alleged sexual assaults, and – unrelated to the unnamed woman’s case – was eventually found guilty on two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution, receiving a four year and two month sentence in October 2025.

The woman said that after making the allegations, she was unaware of the lawsuit being filed on her behalf and, after she expressed doubts about her claims, the lawsuit was dropped.

Jay-Z has previously spoken about the impact the allegations had on his life. When the case was dropped, he said: “The trauma that my wife, my children, loved ones and I have endured can never be dismissed,” and speaking to GQ in March he said: “I haven’t been that angry in a long time, uncontrollable anger. You don’t put that on someone – that’s a thing that you better be super sure [about].”

He said he had refused to settle the lawsuit out of court: “I can’t take a settlement – it ain’t in my DNA … I would die.”
output.standfirst: The woman has withdrawn her 2024 claim that the rapper raped her aged 13, saying her false accusations caused him immense pain; her lawyer says she maintains she was a victim of sexual assault
output.progress: The woman has formally withdrawn her allegation in a declaration and has now been dropped from Jay-Z’s lawsuit.

output.headline: Record security funding reaches UK mosques under hate crime scheme
output.trail: Almost £3m was issued to mosques and associated sites under the places of worship security scheme in the year to April 2023.

output.headline: Home Office report examines what lies behind hate crimes against transgender people
output.trail: Recorded hate crimes against transgender people in England and Wales rose 11 per cent to a record high, an increase the report says may be due to comments in media and by politicians.

output.headline: Germany pledges fossil fuel phase-out by 2045 in what campaigners call notable shift
output.trail: It is the first time Germany has made such a pledge: campaigners say the plan marks a notable shift away from oil and gas, as previous pledges were only for carbon neutrality.

output.headline: Endangered birds win 11th-hour protection from SA space project plans
output.trail: The decision is welcomed for birds 'hanging on by a thread': the Eyre peninsula site is 'precious and important' habitat for the southern emu-wren and home to 80 per cent of mallee whipbirds.

output.headline: How a ceiling design funnels a tropical breeze through Réunion's airport terminal
output.trail: 'We wanted to prove we didn't need air conditioning': Roland Garros airport on Réunion island is cooled by natural ventilation, its ceiling funnelling a light tropical breeze into the terminal.

output.headline: Rick Wakeman plays Vietnam sanctuary concert to raise awareness of caged animals
output.trail: The former Yes musician performs piano to 150 rescued moon bears at the sanctuary, highlighting animals that remain stuck in cages at 'bile farms'.

output.headline: Agreement signed this week brings Greenlanders hope of independence
output.trail: Hopeful Greenlanders breathe a collective sigh of relief after so long in Trump's sights, and locals hope the agreement will end US threats to annex the island.

output.headline: Experts build dog DNA database that could help police catch criminals
output.trail: The database of UK dogs that experts are working on could identify particular breeds involved in crimes, or rule out canine suspects.
